title: DevOps checks

story: A small pull request in the gitops repo, where the Helm charts for the product clusters live, changes one line in the dashboard chart's prod-aws-values.yaml: the number of copies of the dashboard, replicaCount, becomes "two" instead of 2. The diff looks harmless, a reviewer approves it, and nothing in CI checks it, because the gitops repo has no checks at all.

The first program that really reads the file is Argo CD, the tool that applies the charts to the real cluster. It fails to sync production, and someone spends the evening finding a typo that a machine could have found in seconds. Soon agents will open pull requests in this repo and in the infrastructure repo too, many more of them than people do.
hook.question: How can CI check infrastructure code for every environment before any real system reads it, without giving CI any keys to those systems?

read.h: Check it where it is still text
p: Infrastructure code has the same problem as the projects page in the verify lesson: the mistake is in one file, but it only shows up when something reads all the files together. For a Helm chart, that something is rendering. A chart is a set of templates plus a values file per environment, and helm template fills the templates with one values file and prints the Kubernetes manifests, the YAML that a cluster would receive. Nothing is sent anywhere, so rendering needs no cluster and no keys.

Rendering alone is not enough, because replicas: two is still valid YAML. kubeconform reads rendered manifests and checks each one against the Kubernetes API's own schemas, the same rules the cluster would apply, offline. It says replicas must be an integer, which is exactly the error Argo CD hit in production. helm lint, the chart's own linter, does not catch it: it checks that the chart is well formed, not that the result is something a cluster accepts.

code.text:
#!/bin/bash
# Render every environment of the chart and check the result against the Kubernetes schemas, offline.
set -o pipefail  # without it, a chart that does not render at all looks green
status=0
for values in dashboard/*-values.yaml; do
  echo "== $values"
  helm template ci dashboard -f "$values" | docker run --rm -i ghcr.io/yannh/kubeconform:v0.7.0 -strict -summary - || status=1
done
exit $status

notes.text: Without pipefail, the pipe's result is only kubeconform's, and kubeconform says yes to empty input.
Every environment's values file, because a typo in one environment breaks only that one.
Render with one values file and check every manifest; remember the failure but keep going.
One report with every broken environment, and a red exit code if there was any.

read.h: The same idea in every repo
p: The chart check is one example of a general rule: a check that needs no keys can run on every push, from anyone, including an agent, because it cannot change or read any real system. Each repo gets the checks that fit its files. In the infrastructure repo, where our cloud is described in OpenTofu, tofu validate checks every module's types and references after tofu init -backend=false, which skips the state and every credential. tflint finds mistakes validate cannot see, such as an instance type that does not exist, and trivy config scans the code for risky settings such as a security group open to the whole internet.

For CI's own files there is a third pair. actionlint finds broken GitHub workflows, and zizmor finds risky ones, such as a ${{ }} expression that puts outside text into a shell script. Every new check starts in a softer mode where it reports and does not fail, because its first run finds old problems that need an owner. Each problem is then fixed, or written into an ignore file with an owner and a reason, before the check may block a pull request. The files that define these checks are on the list of paths agents may not change, so an agent cannot loosen the check that judges its own pull request.

read.h: When a check must read the real thing
p: Some questions cannot be answered from text alone. A Terraform plan, the list of what an apply would add, change and destroy, has to compare the code with what really exists in the cloud, so it needs credentials. The answer is a role that can read and do nothing else: in each AWS account a TerraformPlanRole with AWS's ReadOnlyAccess policy plus an explicit deny on reading data such as objects, secrets and table rows, because a plan needs configuration, never data. Only pull request runs of the infrastructure repo may take that role.

With it, CI posts the plan of every changed unit as one comment on the pull request, so reviewers and agents see the real effect of a change. It never writes a plan file, because a plan file holds secret values in plain text, and the workflow has no apply, destroy or manual start anywhere. For the gitops repo the same idea is a diff preview: Argo CD's view of main and of the pull request is rendered on a throw-away kind cluster (Kubernetes running inside Docker, gone with the job), and the difference is posted as a comment. In both cases, applying stays a person's job.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why the deny matters
p: ReadOnlyAccess sounds safe, but read access to everything includes the contents of every S3 object, every secret in Secrets Manager and every row in DynamoDB. A plan job runs code from the pull request it is planning, so a malicious or confused change could print those values into a public log. In IAM an explicit deny always beats an allow, so the deny on s3:GetObject, secretsmanager:GetSecretValue, ssm:GetParameter*, kms:Decrypt and DynamoDB reads closes that hole. Units whose data sources need a secret are left out of pull request plans.

lab.title: Every environment, checked offline
needs: Docker running (kubeconform runs from its image)
Internet, once, for the image and kubeconform's schemas
lab.goal: Catch a typo in one environment's values file that helm lint misses, by rendering every environment and checking it against the Kubernetes schemas, then do the same for OpenTofu modules.

guess.q: prod-values.yaml sets replicaCount: two. You run helm lint dashboard -f dashboard/prod-values.yaml. What does it say?

options.why: helm lint checks that the chart is well formed. replicas: two is valid YAML, so lint has nothing to complain about.

options.text: An error: replicas must be an integer
options.why: That is kubeconform's message. Only a schema check knows what a Deployment's replicas field must be.

options.text: A warning that the values file is unknown
options.why: Any values file works with -f. Helm does not judge the values themselves.

solution.text:
#!/bin/bash
# Validate every module without a backend or cloud keys, and report all broken modules, not only the first.
status=0
for dir in modules/*/; do
  if (cd "$dir" && tofu init -backend=false -input=false -no-color >/dev/null && tofu validate -no-color >/dev/null 2>&1); then
    echo "ok    $dir"
  else
    echo "FAIL  $dir"; (cd "$dir" && tofu validate -no-color 2>&1 | grep -E "Error|on main.tf" | head -3)
    status=1
  fi
done
exit $status

lab.fix: A teammate removed the line set -o pipefail from check-charts.sh, saying "the || status=1 already handles failures". Remove it and run ./check-charts.sh with staging-values.yaml still there. Staging now ends with Summary: 0 resource found … Errors: 0, and if you fix prod, the whole check exits with 0, although staging cannot even be rendered. Find why: without pipefail the pipe's exit code is kubeconform's alone, and kubeconform accepts empty input. Put the line back.

Why can these checks run on every agent pull request, while a Terraform plan needs a special read-only role?

check.q: A values change is fine in dev but has a typo in prod-aws-values.yaml. CI renders only the chart's default values.yaml. What happens?

options.text: CI is green, and the typo is found by Argo CD when it syncs production.
options.why: The broken file is never rendered in CI. Rendering every environment's values file is the whole point of the check.

options.text: CI is red, because helm lint reads every values file in the folder.
options.why: helm lint reads the values you give it, and even then it does not check Kubernetes types.

options.text: CI is red, because kubeconform checks values files directly.
options.why: kubeconform checks rendered manifests. It never sees a values file that was not rendered.

check.q: Why may tofu validate, kubeconform and zizmor run on every push, including an agent's, while the plan job needs its own role?

options.text: They are faster than a plan.
options.why: Speed is a bonus. The reason is what they can touch.

options.text: They need no credentials, so they cannot read or change any real system, whoever triggers them.
options.why: A plan must compare the code with the real cloud, so it needs read access, which is why it gets a role that can only read configuration.

options.text: Agents are not allowed to see plans.
options.why: Agents can read the plan comment. What nobody's CI job may do is apply.

check.q: The plan role has ReadOnlyAccess. Why add an explicit deny on s3:GetObject, secretsmanager:GetSecretValue and similar actions?

options.text: Because ReadOnlyAccess cannot list resources without it.
options.why: Listing works either way. The deny removes something, it adds nothing.
It is about what a plan job could leak, not about speed.

options.text: Because read access includes the data itself, and a plan runs code from the pull request, which could print secrets into a log.
options.why: A plan needs configuration, never data. An explicit deny beats any allow in IAM.

p: infrastructure: .github/workflows/terraform-checks.yml next to terrugrunt-lint.yml (same push paths, infrastructure-runner-set, actions pinned by SHA, tenv tofu install) runs tofu init -backend=false and tofu validate per modules/* folder, tflint --recursive with a root .tflint.hcl (aws and google rulesets, GITHUB_TOKEN for plugin downloads; pin the plugin and trivy-action versions), and trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL over modules/, terraform/ and multi_tenant/, advisory for two weeks, then failing on new findings with an owned .trivyignore. gitops: chart-checks.yml on pull_request (gitops-runner-set) runs helm dependency build, helm lint and helm template per *-values.yaml into kubeconform -strict with the datreeio CRDs-catalog for ExternalSecret, ScaledObject, HTTPRoute and Application; set -kubernetes-version to the oldest product cluster's version rather than a fixed 1.36.0.

workflow-lint.yml (actionlint and zizmor --min-severity medium, advisory) goes into fcp, infrastructure, gitops, byte, ai-agents and claude-plugins, with each repo's .github/actionlint.yaml for runner labels and a zizmor.yml that allows tags for actions/* in fcp; look first at comment-triggered workflows such as byte-review.yml. TerraformPlanRole lives in terraform/accounts/<account>/aws/global/iam/terraform-plan/, trusted only by GitHubActionsTerraformPlan in inf, which trusts only repo:RhinoHealth/infrastructure:pull_request; account.hcl reads TG_ROLE_NAME; a read-only Vault role and an EKS view access entry come later, and new accounts get both roles in the manual bootstrap list. terragrunt-plan.yml plans changed units with -lock=false and no -out, and posts one sticky comment. argocd-diff-preview.yml renders argocd-apps for both branches and runs dagandersen/argocd-diff-preview (pinned) on kind inside the dind sidecar, with a read-only token and no cluster credentials.

tickets.why: tofu validate, tflint and trivy config in infrastructure CI, with no keys.
helm lint and helm template | kubeconform for every environment of each changed chart: this lesson.
actionlint and zizmor in every repo with workflows.
The read-only TerraformPlanRole and its OIDC trust for pull request plans.
Read-only Terragrunt plans posted on infrastructure pull requests; never apply.
argocd-diff-preview on a throw-away kind cluster for gitops pull requests.

words.plain: Fills a chart's templates with one values file and prints the Kubernetes manifests, without a cluster.
Checks rendered Kubernetes YAML against the API's schemas, offline.
A check that needs no credentials, so it can run on every push from anyone.
A bash option: a pipe fails if any command in it fails, not only the last one.
A cloud role that can read configuration but no data, used only to compute plans.

review.q: Name one keyless check for each of the three kinds of files: Helm charts, OpenTofu modules and GitHub workflows.
review.a: helm template | kubeconform for charts, tofu validate (or tflint, trivy config) for modules, actionlint (or zizmor) for workflows.

review.q: Why does a new check start in a mode that reports but does not fail?
review.a: Its first run finds old problems. Each needs a fix or an owned ignore entry before the check may block pull requests, or every pull request would be red for problems it did not cause.

review.q: What two things does the plan workflow never do, and why?
review.a: It never writes a plan file (it holds secrets in plain text) and never applies, destroys or starts by hand; applying is a person's job.

remember: Check infrastructure where it is still text, every environment and without keys; when a check must read the real cloud, give it a role that can only read configuration, and leave apply to a person.
